1:
Why so contemptible an instrument is the question the fuller writers all begin with. Henry observes that God could have plagued them with lions or bears or vultures, and chose frogs for two reasons: to magnify his power, since some have thought it as much shown in making an ant as an elephant; and to humble Pharaoh, for what a mortification to be brought to his knees by means every child can ordinarily deal with, yet which all his chariots and horsemen could make no head against. If God be our enemy, Henry adds, all the creatures are at war with us. Clarke reasons the same way from the other end: had crocodiles or lions been used, the effect would have seemed commensurate with the cause and the hand of God might have been forgotten, the people exasperated without being humbled; so God shows his power by making an animal devoid of every evil quality the means of a terrible affliction, the fly in his hands being a sufficient instrument of vengeance. Calvin finds a third motive, that God chose not merely to punish the Egyptians but to expose them to mockery. Their pain must have been embittered by seeing themselves evil-entreated not by a victorious army but by filthy reptiles, and by the calamity rising out of the Nile that had enriched them; if we are galled by ignominy, he says, it happens designedly, to mortify our pride.

Calvin draws a further lesson from their number. Egypt, with its marshes and sluggish river, was always full of frogs, so that when multitudes came forth at once and climbed into the royal palace it plainly appeared they had until then been restrained by God's hand, and that the God of the Hebrews was the guardian of that kingdom.

On the warning Henry and Clarke insist that it was mercy. God does not punish men for sin unless they persist in it, Henry says, and the form of the threat intimates that if Pharaoh complied the controversy would be dropped; Clarke adds that nothing can be plainer than that Pharaoh still had it in his power to dismiss the people, his refusal being the mere effect of wilful obstinacy. Of the river Clarke remarks that the Nile, an object of their adoration, was made an instrument of their punishment, and that bringing forth abundantly suggests the spawn already in the water was brought miraculously to perfection; Wesley takes the river for all the waters of the land, and Gill says the frogs were produced at once, spread over the nation in a day and gone the next. Clarke's most domestic note is on the ovens, which in the East are a hole in the ground holding an earthen pot to whose inside the cakes are stuck, so that to find one full of frogs on coming to heat it must have been distressing.

What the magicians did nobody thinks was creation. Clarke suggests a little juggling sufficed, frogs being already in abundance and some kept ready to be brought forward. Ellicott agrees it was probably sleight-of-hand, and says all the writer means is that they seemed to Pharaoh and the court to do on a small scale what Moses had done on the largest; they would have shown their power and their gods' far better had they taken the frogs away. Keil puts it as a bare contrast, that they could bring the plague but not remove it. Henry takes it for a type, since the unclean spirits that come out of the mouth of the dragon are said to be like frogs, the dragon meaning by them to deceive while God meant by them to destroy those who would be deceived. On the execution Calvin notes that Moses moved not a finger, transferring the work to his inferior minister so that Pharaoh might be treated the more contemptuously.
8:
Ellicott marks this as the first sign of yielding. Pharaoh had borne the water turned to blood without flinching, probably because he suffered little from it himself, but the frogs reached him as much as anyone, and inconvenience drove him to concede; as far as words went the concession was complete, since he acknowledged the power of Jehovah and of righteous men's prayers, and promised to let the people go. Calvin allows that terror may really have driven him to seek pardon, but says the lying is plain from his inconstancy: the moment a reprieve was granted he returned to his natural disposition. So it is with hypocrites: under God's afflicting hand they implore mercy, and when the evil is withdrawn a short truce puffs up their hearts as though they had won an eternal peace, which is the psalm's complaint of the Jews. Calvin finds the double mind in the request itself, Pharaoh making a bargain of it, the frogs to go before the people did; yet that he names Jehovah at all shows the stoutness broken of a spirit that once asked in mockery who the Lord was.

The phrase Moses answers with has puzzled everyone. Clarke reports that the Septuagint and Vulgate both render it appoint unto me when I shall pray, which countenances Le Clerc's conjecture that one letter has been altered. He thinks this the genuine import, since nothing could prove the plague supernatural more fully than Pharaoh being allowed to name the hour of its removal. Ellicott takes them for a courtesy rather than a puzzle, equivalent to saying I submit to thy will, probably an ordinary Egyptian civility, which is why it is no Hebrew idiom and occurs nowhere else. Calvin rejects both readings he knows. Those who make it the honour of fixing a time are too speculative, those who make it the death of the frogs flat; the contrast is rather between Pharaoh's old boasting and the pious glorying he ought to seek. Thus far, Moses is saying, you have exalted yourself wrongly, trusting your power and then bewitched by the enchanters; now glory instead in having an advocate with God.

Why the king said to-morrow is the sharpest question here. Gill gives the two usual answers: he hoped the frogs might go off overnight and leave him beholden to nobody, or he supposed the work needed time for the ceremonies his magicians used. Wesley takes the first, Ellicott and Keil the second, guessing he thought even Jehovah could not do so great a thing at once. Calvin denies the whole construction. Those fall into an absurdity who suppose Pharaoh asked that the frogs be driven off on the morrow, as though he went quietly to sleep and postponed his own relief; he was asking a respite before letting the people go, suspending it for deceit's sake, so that having got what he wanted he might break his engagement. The frogs, Calvin holds, went the same day, since what changed the tyrant's mind was that a night's interval carried his fear away.

Clarke notes that killing them mitigated the plague while leaving them to rot kept it in view, and thinks Calmet's conjecture rational, that the flies of the next plague bred from ova laid in the heaps, God never working a miracle where nature will serve. On the hardening all three lay the act on Pharaoh. Ellicott says Pharaoh's nature had until now not been impressed, his heart dull and callous, and that an impression having been made he must have yielded had he not called in his own will to efface it, which was his great guilt; Wesley says flatly that he did it himself, God no otherwise than by not hindering; Calvin has him twisting like a serpent to crooked counsels, God having foreknown the perfidy and remitted the punishment to bring it to light.
16:
Henry notes that no warning preceded this plague, and thinks Pharaoh's abuse of the respite was warning enough: if the removal of an affliction hardens us, it goes away meaning to return, or to make room for worse. He and Wesley both mark the change of material — the frogs came out of the water, these out of the dust — since out of any part of the creation God can fetch a scourge. Calvin hears the affront. God trampled on the pride of Egypt by a punishment full of disgrace, since it would have been painful to sink under a warlike enemy but far sadder to be basely destroyed by lice; no animal is so vile that it cannot injure when God employs it, and this is what the proud come to, yielding with infamy to worms.

What the creatures were nobody settles. Calvin says the Hebrews do not agree, but grant they were small insects bringing shame as well as annoyance to the meanest men. Clarke canvasses the field: the Septuagint and Vulgate make them gnats; Harmer would have the stinging tarrentes of an old crusading chronicle, which Clarke calls far-fetched; Bochart argues for lice on four grounds: these sprang from dust not water, they were on men and cattle alike, the root of the name means to fix, which can never suit creatures always on the wing, and the Talmudists use the same word for the louse. Clarke's own verdict goes further: their being in man and in beast fits the tick so exactly, an insect that buries sucker and head in the flesh and will be pulled to pieces rather than let go, that he takes it for the creature meant. Ellicott and Keil read mosquitoes throughout.

Why the magicians failed is answered several ways. Ellicott has them take moist earth, dry and pulverise it and try their charms on it, failing because mosquitoes are too delicate to be produced at a given moment by sleight-of-hand. Clarke reasons from the effect rather than the creature: insects were required that would stick and infix themselves in man and beast, which no trick could imitate; and if the magicians did act by spiritual agents, those agents plainly had assigned limits. Calvin takes the verb itself to mean they tried and failed, and sees God taking away the last pretext of being deceived, since Pharaoh's obstinacy had colour of excuse while the magicians could rival Moses, but none once their art failed; when God has borne with Satan's ministers long enough to prove his people's faith, he compels them to proceed no further.

What they meant by the finger of God divides the readings sharply. Ellicott renders it the finger of a god and says they meant only that this lay beyond the power of man and some god must be helping Moses, with no profession of belief in one God; Gill notices that they said Elohim and not Jehovah, whom on Lightfoot's account they reckoned a petty local deity, so the confession detracted at once from Moses and from the God of Israel. Keil makes the same point structurally: their seeing only some deity, possibly an Egyptian one, is why the later plagues began to distinguish Israel from Egypt, which proved whose hand it was. Henry and Wesley take the confession at its face, drawing the moral that God has the devil in a chain and limits him as deceiver and destroyer alike, so the magicians' failure here shows whence their earlier power came; sooner or later God extorts from his enemies an acknowledgment of his sovereignty, as the dying apostate owned that the Galilean had overcome him. Ellicott ends with the plainest explanation of Pharaoh's unconcern: the insects did not impress him as the frogs had, and he needed no act of will to harden himself, having curtains and rooms above the height they rise to.
20:
Henry and Wesley both take the order to rise early as a rebuke. Those who would bring great things to pass for God and their generation must redeem the morning, since Pharaoh was early up at his superstitious devotions to the river; shall we be for more sleep when service is to be done that would pass well in our account at the great day? Henry adds that a faithful servant must not fear the face of man, Moses being sent to challenge a proud king, if he kept his captives, to engage an army of flies. Calvin thinks the riverside was chosen so nothing should be done secretly, Moses proclaiming the judgment in open day before the multitude.

What the creatures were is again disputed, along the same lines as the lice. Keil follows the Septuagint's dog-fly, noting that these are far more numerous and annoying than gnats and, when enraged, fasten on the body and especially the edges of the eyelids. Clarke gives Bochart's case for the same reading and grants its weight, since the dog-fly would be peculiarly hateful to a people who venerated dogs and worshipped Anubis under a dog's form, and since the Septuagint's translators worked in the very country where the plagues happened. Yet he inclines to the literal sense of the root, which is to mingle, since the same word at the exodus describes the mixed multitude that went up with Israel, so a swarm of many kinds — flies, wasps, hornets — is likelier; Wesley reads it so, and thinks them more pernicious than common. Calvin traces the same root, from which evening takes its name because day and night are mingled in it, and which also names a mixed crowd; he allows many kinds and rejects only the beasts.

The severing of Goshen draws two questions, of the word and of the fact. Clarke reports that good critics render it I will miraculously separate, the Vulgate having I will do a marvellous thing and the Septuagint I will render illustrious; Calvin knows the same alternative, the root bearing both to divide and to be admirable, but prefers the usual rendering. Of the fact Ellicott is clearest. Goshen can only have been part of the eastern Delta, a tract in no way different from the rest of Egypt, low and flat and well watered; nature had put no severance between it and the Egyptians' country, so the severance now made would be a manifest miracle. Henry says as much historically, the distinction having not been so observable in any earlier plague.

On the second word all agree against the old versions. Keil states it flatly: the term does not mean division, as the Septuagint and Vulgate have it, but redemption, exemption from the plague being a deliverance that marked the distinction conferred on Israel. Gill and Clarke render it redemption too, Clarke saying God thereby showed he had redeemed them from plagues to which he abandoned the rest, Gill carrying it forward to the difference God makes between his chosen and the world by his Son's redemption; Wesley keeps the plainer figure of a wall of partition. Henry and Wesley draw the same demonstration from the flies' obedience: creatures that seem to fly at random are manifestly under an intelligent mind while above the direction of any man, so that when Moses says hither they shall go and thither they shall not come, and the event answers punctually, the two prove that he who said it and he who did it were one. Calvin notes that the morrow was named rather than the moment so time for repentance might be given again, and the tyrant's wickedness proved. Keil describes what came: the land was desolated, the flies not only torturing and devouring the people and disfiguring them with swellings, but killing the plants in which they laid their eggs.
25:
Ellicott explains why the king gave way so quickly, without waiting for the magicians to remonstrate: the swarms were on him personally with their painful bites, in his palaces destroying rich furniture, and over his lands. Ellicott says Pharaoh mars all by one little clause, a three days' journey having been demanded from the first and nothing less being acceptable; Clarke puts the offer plainly: they should not leave Egypt but have their worship tolerated there. Calvin makes this the type of a permanent fault. Pharaoh imagines he is granting a great thing, yet renounces no idol, merely allowing God to be worshipped in one corner of his kingdom; and it is customary with the reprobate to think they have done their duty when they yield ever so little. While fortune is propitious they deprive God of all his glory, and when resistance fails they submit only so far as to defraud him of half his due; our own Pharaohs, having failed to extinguish that glory outright, maim his worship by a fictitious course which they call a reformation, whence came that mixture of light and darkness named the Interim.

Why sacrificing in Egypt was impossible is explained twice. Clarke says the animals the Egyptians held sacred were precisely those the Hebrew rites required, few people having ever been more superstitious, almost every production of nature being an object of worship — sun and moon, the Nile, beasts from the monkey to the ibis, and even the onions and leeks in their gardens. Ellicott makes the danger concrete. Sheep, goats and cattle, the whole Hebrew sacrificial list, were sacred either generally or in particular districts, so a Theban could not endure the killing of a sheep nor a Mendesian of a goat; any bull-calf might prove an Apis, which could not be known until the priests examined him. He shows what such a killing cost by two incidents: a Roman ambassador who killed a cat by accident was torn to pieces, and war broke out between two towns because one ate a fish the other held sacred. The fear of Moses, he concludes, was not groundless.

Calvin questions which way the phrase runs. The Hebrews say of whatever they disapprove that it is not right, and almost all interpreters take Pharaoh to have demanded what was inequitable, exposing the Israelites to stoning. Calvin finds two clauses rather than one, and a twofold argument: the thing was not right, and it was not expedient. Set against the name of Jehovah, the abomination may mean the profanation with which Egyptian ceremonies were defiled, so the first reason is that a sacrifice polluted by them would please God no more than it was lawful, and only the second that the Egyptians would not tolerate the sight. He refuses too to restrict the word to the sacrificial animals, extending it to the whole act, and insists that Moses looked first to God's honour, not merely the people's safety.

On the wilderness Clarke and Wesley agree that neither Moses nor Aaron yet knew how God would be worshipped, expecting a revelation once they arrived; Calvin praises the firmness that rejected the tyrant's pretended moderation, no change being permissible in a divine command. Keil observes that the reasons commended themselves to the heathen king on his own religious ground, so he conceded the wilderness. Clarke sees the concession for what it was worth: Pharaoh relented because God's hand was heavy on him, but would not give up his gain, the Israelites being state slaves whose labour was productive; how ready is foolish man under pressure to compound with his Maker, giving up some sins if he may keep the rest. His request for intercession Clarke likens to Simon Magus begging an interest in Peter's prayers; Gill notes that the king avoided naming the three days, though the journey he allowed could not be made in less.
29:
Ellicott explains why Moses let the qualifying clause pass. He had stated his demand plainly for a three days' journey, and it was for Pharaoh to settle whether that counted as very far; since the king raised no clear objection, Moses was bound to suppose he allowed it. The warning that followed Ellicott holds was owed: God's servants must rebuke even kings who openly break the moral law, and Pharaoh had promised unconditionally to release the people, then broken his word. Calvin looks at what Moses did not say. He gave no answer because he knew God's design was otherwise, God having justly left him ignorant of what he did not yet wish him to know; there is no ground for charging him with bad faith over a silence he was not ordered to break. Roused by the king's perfidy, he does not remove the plague at once but waits till the morrow, threatening punishment if the deceit continues — an extraordinary boldness, to reproach a tyrant to his face and menace him in the same breath, gathered from the miracles in which he had proved God's unconquerable power.

Calvin adds a caution: Moses spoke from a special impulse, not from his own mind, the general promise that God grants his servants' prayers not applying to particular cases unless a man has peculiar testimony from the word or Spirit. On the fulfilment he notes that the word God performed may be either the answer or the prayer of Moses, and prefers the former, that by the result God ratified what he had said, having made him proclaimer of his judgment. Clarke draws the plainer moral, that prayer is powerful when God lets his servant prescribe the manner and time of his working, and guesses that a strong wind swept the swarms into the sea. Ellicott marks the completeness as itself miraculous: the entire removal of such a plague at a word was almost as great a wonder as its coming, which is why it is carefully recorded, nothing of the sort being said of the frogs or the gnats.

On the final hardening the voices converge. Clarke calls it the mere effect of self-determining obstinacy, Pharaoh preferring his gain to the will of Jehovah, and God making that obstinacy the means of showing his own power; Ellicott notes that here again it is after being impressed and partly relenting that the king hardens his own heart; Wesley says it is still his own act, not God's; Gill assigns the motive to pride and covetousness, the king being loath to lose so large a branch of his revenues. Calvin finds the phrase at this time also an aggravation, since there was no bound to a rebellion holding out under such punishments, by which even an iron heart should have been corrected.

Clarke closes with a summary of what these plagues proved. As every false religion argues a true one, being a marred copy of some original, so false miracles argue genuine. These were genuine: the water was not turned to blood in appearance only, since the people could not drink it and the fish died, and no human ingenuity could have produced such frogs. Only to superficial observers, he insists, do Moses and the magicians appear nearly matched. They could sometimes imitate a plague but never remove one, and though they produced serpents could bring none that would swallow Aaron's rod; their opposition served only as a foil to the power by which God's messengers acted. From all this, he concludes, learn that God works in the earth and can invert its general laws when he pleases, saving or destroying by the most contemptible instruments, and that he has not so bound himself to them as to exclude a particular providence — Egypt was ruined while in all Goshen there was no blood in the streams and neither frog nor fly.
